title: Basic Nursing Care — Mobility, Positioning, Transfers & ROM (Set 7)
subtitle: Complications of immobility, range of motion & contractures, safe transfers, gait belts & mechanical lifts, wheelchair/walker safety, positioning & DVT recognition
scenario: Keeping clients safely mobile—preventing the complications of immobility, performing range-of-motion, positioning clients correctly, transferring and ambulating them safely with belts, lifts, and assistive devices, and recognizing problems such as deep vein thrombosis.

steps.q: Prolonged immobility can lead to which serious complications the technician should help prevent?

opts.text: Blood clots (DVT), pneumonia, muscle wasting, and joint contractures
opts.rat: Immobility increases the risk of deep vein thrombosis, respiratory problems like pneumonia, loss of muscle strength, and contractures, among other complications—so promoting safe movement matters.

opts.text: Improved circulation and lung function
opts.rat: Immobility tends to impair, not improve, circulation and lung function.

opts.text: Stronger muscles and joints
opts.rat: Immobility leads to muscle weakening and stiff joints, not strengthening.

opts.text: No effect on the body at all
opts.rat: Immobility has many harmful effects on nearly every body system.

steps.q: 'Passive' range-of-motion exercises are:

opts.text: Movements the client does entirely on their own
opts.rat: When the client does the movement themselves, it is active range-of-motion.

opts.text: Movements the technician or caregiver performs for a client who cannot move the joint themselves
opts.rat: Passive range-of-motion is performed by the caregiver for a client who cannot move the joint on their own, helping maintain joint flexibility.

opts.text: Only done during physical therapy sessions
opts.rat: Passive ROM can be part of routine care, not only formal therapy.

opts.text: A type of medication
opts.rat: Range-of-motion is a physical exercise, not a medication.

steps.q: 'Active' range-of-motion means:

opts.text: The technician moves the joints while the client stays still
opts.rat: That describes passive range-of-motion, not active.

opts.text: The joints are never moved
opts.rat: Range-of-motion involves moving the joints; active means the client does it.

opts.text: The client performs the joint movements themselves
opts.rat: In active range-of-motion the client moves their own joints, which helps maintain both mobility and strength.

opts.text: Movement is done only with a machine
opts.rat: Active ROM is performed by the client, not by a machine.

steps.q: When performing range-of-motion exercises, the technician should:

opts.text: Force each joint well past the point of resistance
opts.rat: Forcing past resistance can injure the joint; movement should be gentle.

opts.text: Move quickly and jerkily to finish fast
opts.rat: Fast, jerky movements can cause injury; ROM is done slowly and smoothly.

opts.text: Continue even when the client reports sharp pain
opts.rat: Sharp pain is a signal to stop; ROM should not be pushed into pain.

opts.text: Move each joint slowly and gently to the point of resistance, without forcing past pain
opts.rat: Range-of-motion is performed slowly and gently, moving each joint to the point of resistance but not forcing beyond it or into pain.

steps.q: The main purpose of range-of-motion exercises is to:

opts.text: Maintain joint mobility and prevent contractures and stiffness
opts.rat: Range-of-motion keeps joints flexible, maintains mobility, and helps prevent contractures and stiffness caused by immobility.

opts.text: Replace the client's need for any repositioning
opts.rat: ROM does not replace repositioning; both are part of care.

opts.text: Cure underlying diseases
opts.rat: ROM maintains function; it does not cure underlying disease.

opts.text: Increase the client's blood pressure
opts.rat: Raising blood pressure is not the purpose of ROM.

steps.q: A 'contracture' is:

opts.text: A temporary muscle cramp that resolves in minutes
opts.rat: A contracture is not a brief cramp; it is a lasting shortening of tissue.

opts.text: A permanent shortening and tightening of a muscle or joint from lack of movement
opts.rat: A contracture is a permanent tightening/shortening of muscle, tendon, or joint tissue that can result from prolonged immobility; preventing it is a key reason for ROM and positioning.

opts.text: A type of skin rash
opts.rat: A contracture affects muscle/joint tissue, not the skin as a rash.

opts.text: A normal, healthy joint
opts.rat: A contracture is an abnormal, restricting condition, not a healthy joint.

steps.q: A gait (transfer) belt is used during ambulation or transfers to:

opts.text: Restrain the client to the bed
opts.rat: A gait belt is a support/safety aid for movement, not a restraint device.

opts.text: Replace the need for the technician to be present
opts.rat: The belt is used by the technician who stays with the client; it does not replace their presence.

opts.text: Give the technician a secure hold to steady and support the client and help prevent falls
opts.rat: A gait belt around the client's waist gives the technician a secure grip to steady and support the client during transfers and ambulation, reducing fall risk.

opts.text: Measure the client's waist for clothing
opts.rat: A gait belt is a mobility safety aid, not a measuring tool.

steps.q: When ambulating a client who has one-sided (e.g., left-leg) weakness, the technician generally positions themselves:

opts.text: Far away, out of reach
opts.rat: Staying out of reach would prevent the technician from supporting or catching the client.

opts.text: Directly in front, blocking the client's path
opts.rat: Standing directly in front blocks movement and does not support the weak side.

opts.text: Behind and to the side of the client's stronger side only
opts.rat: The technician generally supports the weaker side to guard against a fall toward it.

opts.text: On the client's weaker (affected) side, using a gait belt, to support and guard them
opts.rat: The technician typically stands on the client's weaker/affected side (slightly behind), using a gait belt, so they can support and guard the client if the weak side gives way. (Confirm the exact technique with faculty.)

steps.q: Before transferring a client into or out of a wheelchair, the technician must FIRST:

opts.text: Lock the wheelchair brakes and move the footrests out of the way
opts.rat: Locking the brakes keeps the wheelchair from rolling, and moving the footrests aside prevents tripping and injury—both essential before a transfer.

opts.text: Leave the brakes unlocked so the chair can move freely
opts.rat: An unlocked chair can roll away during transfer, causing a fall.

opts.text: Leave the footrests down and in the way
opts.rat: Footrests left down are a trip/injury hazard during transfer.

opts.text: Remove the client's non-skid footwear
opts.rat: Non-skid footwear should be on for safe transfers, not removed.

steps.q: For a client who is heavy or fully dependent and cannot bear weight, the safest way to move them is to:

opts.text: Lift the client alone as quickly as possible
opts.rat: Lifting a dependent client alone risks injury to both the client and the technician.

opts.text: Use a mechanical lift and/or get adequate help, following safe-handling policy
opts.rat: Dependent clients who cannot bear weight should be moved with a mechanical lift and/or sufficient staff, following safe patient-handling policy, to protect the client and staff from injury.

opts.text: Drag the client by the arms
opts.rat: Dragging by the arms can injure the client's shoulders and skin and is unsafe.

opts.text: Have the client transfer with no assistance
opts.rat: A fully dependent client cannot safely transfer without assistance.

steps.q: When a client who has been lying down is going to stand, the technician should first:

opts.text: Have them jump straight up to standing
opts.rat: Standing up suddenly can cause a drop in blood pressure and dizziness.

opts.text: Keep them lying flat and pull them upright quickly
opts.rat: A quick move from flat to standing risks orthostatic dizziness and injury.

opts.text: Let them sit and dangle their legs at the bedside briefly before standing, to prevent dizziness
opts.rat: Allowing the client to sit and dangle their legs for a short time lets blood pressure adjust and reduces dizziness from orthostatic (postural) hypotension before standing.

opts.text: Have them stand and immediately walk quickly
opts.rat: Standing and rushing to walk increases the risk of a fall from dizziness.

steps.q: Correct use of a standard walker involves the client:

opts.text: Placing the walker far ahead and lunging toward it
opts.rat: Reaching too far and lunging is unstable and increases fall risk.

opts.text: Lifting the walker overhead between steps
opts.rat: The walker is used at ground level for support, not lifted overhead.

opts.text: Leaning the whole body weight backward away from the walker
opts.rat: Leaning backward away from the walker is unstable and unsafe.

opts.text: Moving the walker a short distance forward, then stepping toward it while all legs/tips are stable on the ground
opts.rat: The client advances the walker a short, controlled distance with all tips on the ground for stability, then steps toward it—keeping support throughout. (Confirm the specific gait technique with faculty.)

steps.q: Having a client wear non-skid (non-slip) footwear during ambulation primarily helps to:

opts.text: Prevent slips and falls
opts.rat: Non-skid footwear improves traction on the floor, helping prevent slips and falls during walking and transfers.

opts.text: Improve the client's appearance only
opts.rat: The purpose is safety/traction, not appearance.

opts.text: Make the client walk faster
opts.rat: The goal is safe footing, not increased speed.

opts.text: Replace the need for any assistance
opts.rat: Footwear supports safety but does not replace needed assistance.

steps.q: To help prevent footdrop in a client on prolonged bed rest, the technician can:

opts.text: Leave the feet unsupported and pointed downward
opts.rat: Leaving the feet pointed down (plantar flexed) unsupported contributes to footdrop.

opts.text: Support the feet in a neutral position (for example, with a footboard or supportive device) and use ROM
opts.rat: Keeping the feet supported in a neutral position—such as with a footboard or approved device—along with range-of-motion helps prevent footdrop. (Confirm the specific device/method with faculty.)

opts.text: Keep heavy bedding pressing the toes downward
opts.rat: Heavy bedding pushing the toes down promotes, rather than prevents, footdrop.

opts.text: Avoid moving the ankles at all
opts.rat: Ankle range-of-motion helps prevent footdrop; immobilizing the ankles does not.

steps.q: To keep a client in proper body alignment while in bed, the technician:

opts.text: Twists the client's spine and limbs into awkward positions
opts.rat: Awkward, twisted positions strain the body and can cause harm.

opts.text: Leaves the client in one position indefinitely
opts.rat: Clients need repositioning; staying in one position too long causes complications.

opts.text: Uses pillows and supports to maintain natural alignment and prevent strain
opts.rat: Pillows and supportive devices help keep the head, spine, and limbs in natural alignment, preventing strain, deformity, and pressure.

opts.text: Removes all support so the client lies completely flat and rigid
opts.rat: Supports are used to maintain comfortable, natural alignment, not removed.

steps.q: When transferring a client with one-sided weakness from bed to a chair, it is generally best to position the chair:

opts.text: Far from the bed so the client walks a long way
opts.rat: The chair should be close to allow a short, safe transfer.

opts.text: Behind the client where they cannot see it
opts.rat: The client should be able to see and reach the chair for a safe transfer.

opts.text: So the client must pivot toward their weaker side
opts.rat: Moving toward the weaker side is less stable; leading with the stronger side is safer.

opts.text: On the client's stronger (unaffected) side, so they move toward their stronger side
opts.rat: Placing the chair on the client's stronger side lets them lead and bear weight with the unaffected side, making the transfer safer and more stable. (Confirm technique with faculty.)

steps.q: Which finding in a client's leg should the technician report as a possible blood clot (deep vein thrombosis)?

opts.text: New swelling, redness, warmth, or pain in the calf or leg
opts.rat: New unilateral swelling, redness, warmth, or pain/tenderness in the calf or leg can indicate a deep vein thrombosis and should be reported promptly.

opts.text: Both legs looking their normal size and color
opts.rat: Normal, symmetric legs are not a warning sign.

opts.text: The client walking comfortably
opts.rat: Comfortable walking is not a sign of a clot.

opts.text: Cool, pink, comfortable feet
opts.rat: Warm, painful swelling—not cool, comfortable feet—is the concern for DVT.

steps.q: If the technician suspects a client has a deep vein thrombosis (a swollen, warm, painful calf), they should:

opts.text: Vigorously massage or rub the area to improve circulation
opts.rat: Massaging or rubbing a suspected clot is dangerous—it could dislodge the clot. This must be avoided.

opts.text: Report it promptly and NOT massage or rub the area
opts.rat: A suspected DVT should be reported promptly, and the area must not be massaged or rubbed, because that could dislodge the clot.

opts.text: Have the client vigorously exercise the leg
opts.rat: Vigorous activity on a suspected clot is unsafe; report and follow direction instead.

opts.text: Ignore it unless the client complains repeatedly
opts.rat: A suspected DVT is potentially serious and should be reported promptly, not ignored.

steps.q: Encouraging appropriate activity and early mobility (as allowed) benefits the client by:

opts.text: Increasing the risk of every complication
opts.rat: Appropriate mobility reduces, rather than increases, complications of immobility.

opts.text: Weakening the muscles and lungs
opts.rat: Activity strengthens muscles and supports lung function.

opts.text: Improving circulation, breathing, and digestion and helping prevent complications of immobility
opts.rat: Appropriate activity and early mobility improve circulation, respiratory function, and digestion, and help prevent clots, pneumonia, constipation, and muscle loss.

opts.text: Having no benefit for the client
opts.rat: Mobility has many well-established benefits.

steps.q: During all transfers and mobility assistance, the technician should:

opts.text: Attempt every move alone to prove independence
opts.rat: Working beyond safe limits alone risks injury; getting help is safer.

opts.text: Ignore the client's abilities and limits
opts.rat: Care must be based on the client's specific abilities and limits.

opts.text: Skip safety checks to save time
opts.rat: Skipping safety checks (brakes, footwear, help) endangers the client and technician.

opts.text: Use safe technique, assess the client's ability, get help when needed, and protect both the client's and their own safety
opts.rat: Safe mobility care means using proper technique, assessing what the client can do, obtaining help or equipment when needed, and protecting both the client's and the technician's safety.

reference: Aligned to the California BVNPT Psychiatric Technician exam content area: Basic Nursing Care (mobility, positioning, transfers & range of motion). Written from standard psychiatric-technician and nursing references. Technique specifics—standing on the weaker side during ambulation, walker gait, footboard/footdrop prevention, and chair placement on the stronger side for transfers—follow facility policy and are marked for faculty confirmation. No specific numeric values are asserted. Complements body-mechanics, cane use, and pressure-injury repositioning items already covered in Set 2. Pending faculty review.
